summary: Intro call focused on network isolation and compliance constraints for deploying Redwood Private inside Lighthouse Bio VPC and on-prem datacenter. Main concerns: strict egress governance, SSO/RBAC integration, KMS/HSM key control, and audit log retention for SOC2. Agreed next steps: exchange diagrams, schedule workshop, and start a constrained pilot in a segmented subnet behind egress proxies.
transcript:
[15:19] Meeting start. Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[15:20] Ana (CISO): Ana here. Raj, Kim, Joel - here.
[15:20] Ethan (SE): Ethan from Redwood. I'll lead the technical bits.
[15:21] Maya: Great — agenda is network isolation, egress controls, key management and logging for Redwood Private. We also wanted to surface typical patterns customers use for SOC2 readiness.
[15:21] Ana: Great. Our ask up front: we need strict control of any outbound connections from the model hosts. No unexpected external egress.
[15:22] Raj: To add, our security team requires allowlisting by destination IPs and FQDNs and a signed audit trail to our Splunk instance.
[15:22] Ethan: Understood. Redwood Private supports two deployment profiles — private VPC with customer-controlled NAT/egress, or on-prem where the control plane is air-gapped except for agreed endpoints. For VPC we can supply stable egress ranges but if you run a NAT gateway we can also work with private link endpoints.
[15:23] Joel: When you say "stable egress ranges" — are those static IPs we can add to our firewall?
[15:23] Ethan: Yes, we can provide a small set of CIDR ranges or static elastic IPs depending on the model of deployment. For dedicated setups you'll get more static IPs; hosted is more dynamic.
[15:24] Ana: We need CMK control for encryption — the keys must be in our KMS and rotated per our policy. How does Redwood handle CMKs?
[15:24] Ethan: Redwood Private supports customer-managed keys where the CMK is in your KMS (KMS/HSM). We use envelope encryption: the runtime requests a short-lived data key from your KMS and never persists the plaintext. We can support AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, and HSM-backed keys via KMIP in on-prem.
[15:25] Maya: Quick note — we'll include our KMS integration guide in the follow-up pack.
[15:25] Raj (muttering): okay, that's promising.
[15:26] Kim (Legal): Also need clarity on log retention and what Redwood stores. SOC2 will want access to audit logs and evidence of data handling.
[15:26] Sofia (CSM): We can provide audit logs for model request metadata (timestamps, model version, token counts, requester id) and admin actions from the control plane. Logs can be forwarded to customer SIEM via syslog or cloud-native streaming.
[15:27] Ana: Does that include redaction options? We have PHI concerns.
[15:27] Ethan: Yes — you can enable request-level redaction and sampling for logs in the config. For PHI we recommend filtering at the proxy level; Redwood can accept pre-scrubbed requests, or we can provide inline redaction rules, but that does require some tuning.
[15:28] Joel: On the network side — what do customers typically run for egress filtering? We have an on-prem proxy cluster and a cloud egress proxy.
[15:28] Ethan: Common pattern: all model hosts live in a segmented private subnet with host-level firewalls + egress proxies. Egress goes to a proxy cluster which enforces allowlist/FQDN rules and TLS inspection as required. For cloud, customers use private endpoints (S3 VPC endpoints) and customer-managed NATs with strict route tables. For on-prem, a dedicated DMZ with strict ACLs is common.
[15:29] Raj: Could we run Redwood behind our existing egress proxy without opening raw internet to the hosts?
[15:29] Ethan: Yes — Redwood can be constrained so that the only outbound is to your egress proxy; the proxy then handles the external requests to model stores/observability endpoints. We'll need the proxy to allow the Redwood runtime to reach the KMS endpoints and any monitoring ingestion endpoints.
[15:30] Ana: What about remote code execution risks — do you run any remote auto-updates that hit the internet?
[15:30] Ethan: For Private, updates are controlled by your ops team — we ship artifacts via signed bundles and you can opt for air-gapped installs. If you enable automatic updates, those call home to Redwood-managed endpoints; otherwise you pull updates from a signed artifact repository hosted in your network.
[15:31] Speaker 4: (inaudible)
[15:32] Maya: On identity — we support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning for RBAC. You can map groups to admin roles and create least-privilege tokens.
[15:32] Kim: Can we rotate admin credentials and have offboarding automatically revoke tokens?
[15:33] Ethan: Yes, SCIM-based deprovisioning revokes access downstream; session token TTLs are also configurable. For added assurance we support short-lived certs via your internal PKI for service identities.
[15:34] Raj: Audit pipeline — we'd like to push logs to Splunk with guaranteed ordering and tamper-evidence.
[15:34] Sofia: We have integrations that stream to your SIEM with signing and sequence numbers; we can also hand over S3 log buckets with object lock for immutability if you prefer offline ingestion.
[15:35] Ana: For SOC2 we'll need evidence of network zone separation. Can you provide an example segmentation diagram?
[15:35] Maya: Yes — we have standard VPC diagram templates (control plane in separate account, model hosts in isolated subnets, bastions, egress proxies). We'll send the diagram and an example NACL/security group set.
[15:36] Joel: Are host-level protections supported — like selinux, hardened kernels, eBPF tracing?
[15:36] Ethan: We recommend a defense-in-depth approach. Our deployment packages include recommended sysctl hardening, AppArmor/SELinux policies, and a suggested eBPF observability shim. We don't enforce kernel modules but provide validated configs for your platform team to apply.
[15:37] Kim: Data residency question: if we run in your private deployment in us-west, can logs or backups transit through other regions? Not allowed.
[15:37] Ethan: We have region pinning. All control plane metadata and backups can be configured to stay in a single region. For on-prem, nothing leaves unless explicitly configured. We'll include the data residency section in the pack.
[15:38] Raj: Firewall specifics — do you recommend stateful SGs only, or also host iptables rules?
[15:38] Ethan: Both. SGs/NSGs are your first line; host iptables (or nftables) adds a second layer for defense against misconfigured cloud controls. For high-security customers we ship example iptables rules that drop unknown outbound ports and allow only KMS, NTP, your egress proxy, and monitoring endpoints.
[15:39] Ana: What about non-IP egress such as DNS over HTTPS or CDN interfaces that may complicate allowlisting?
[15:39] Ethan: We prefer FQDN allowlisting on the proxy and blocking direct DoH at the host level. For CDNs, use signed S3 endpoints or direct VPC endpoints where possible to avoid broad CDN ranges.
[15:40] Joel: Is mutual TLS supported between runtime nodes and the control plane?
[15:40] Ethan: Yes — mTLS with client certs issued by your CA is supported. We can also provide SPIFFE-compatible workloads.
[15:41] Maya: Quick check — any mandatory compliance items we haven't covered?
[15:41] Kim: Encryption at rest and in transit, KMS control, audit log retention and proof, RBAC/SSO, and network zone proof — that covers the must-haves. Also we need a runbook describing incident response procedures for exfil attempts.
[15:42] Ethan: We have an incident response playbook and can map roles to your SOC. We'll include a sample runbook and example alerting thresholds.
[15:43] Raj: Performance question — does restricting egress to a proxy add latency to inference?
[15:43] Ethan: Minimal if proxy is co-located (same AZ). We recommend colocating proxies in each zone and using internal LBs; the added hop is ~5-15ms typically. For low-latency use cases we also support cache / prefix caching to reduce external fetches.
[15:44] Ana: OK, pilot scope? We want a small pilot in a restricted subnet that can only reach our Splunk and KMS.
[15:44] Maya: Sounds good. Proposal: one subnet with 3 model hosts, egress only to your proxy and KMS, logs forwarded to Splunk. SE to run initial config and we'll do a security review after 2 weeks.
[15:45] Ethan: I'll draft the exact security group rules and a host hardening checklist.
[15:46] Kim: Legal will need to review the SOC2 packet and the data processing addendum.
[15:46] Maya: We'll attach SOC2 Type II and the DPA.
[15:47] Ana: On monitoring retention — we require 12 months for audit logs and 90 days for detailed trace telemetry. Can you meet that?
[15:47] Sofia: Yes — retention is configurable; we can keep aggregated metrics longer and raw traces for 90 days, and sync logs to your S3 with 12 months retention.
[15:48] Raj: One more — do you support IPsec tunnels for on-prem to cloud control plane?
[15:48] Ethan: We support IPsec and direct private connectivity options. For high-security installs we recommend a VPN with BGP or a direct connect / express route equivalent.
[15:49] Maya: Any final questions?
[15:50] Ana: Not right now. We'll review the artifacts and confirm the workshop time.
[15:51] Maya: Great — recap of next steps and action owners will be in the follow-up. Thanks everyone.
[15:52] Meeting end.
